newsitem.title: USA: Canada spot natgas extends gains on cold, IT cuts.
newsitem.headline: Canada spot natgas extends gains on cold, IT cuts.

text.p: Canadian spot natural gas prices soared to year-high levels Tuesday, led by severely cold temperatures in western Canada and supply cuts on a major pipeline system in British Columbia, sources said.

Prices for Wednesday at Sumas, Wash., on the U.S.-Canada border, jumped more than 70 cents to around $3 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) due to a lack of interruptible transportation on Westcoast's system and bitter cold in the area.

Delivery of "interruptible" (IT) gas, unlike "firm" gas, can be cut when demand exceeds the capacity of the lines needed to carry it to market. For this reason, interruptible gas typically sells at a discount to firm gas.
"We are cutting to firm only," Westcoast Energy's spokeswoman Pat Bowles said Tuesday, adding that about 1.6 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) of firm gas is currently flowing.
"There are supply shortfalls, and it's very cold here," she said, noting the supply cuts are in effect for Wednesday's deliveries.
Current Sumas prices compare with November 1 levels around $2.15 per mmBtu and early September values around $1.00.
At AECO storage hub, prices were up more than 10 cents to the C$2.14-2.22 per gigajoule (GJ) range, with most deals confirmed done around C$2.15.
December AECO prices were talked in the C$2.17-2.19 per GJ range, while the January market hovered around C$2.21, traders said.
Below-freezing temperatures and windy, snowy weather is forecast to continue in Alberta through the week.

At Niagara, the eastern Canadian export point, prices for Wednesday delivery firmed more than 10 cents to the low-to-mid $3.30s per mmBtu as the region anticipated below-normal temperatures by Thursday.
Exacerbating the tight supply situation are the low storage supplies in the western U.S.

According to the American Gas Association, working gas stocks in the West were only at 69 percent of capacity as of November 8. Traders said they expect the data to show another drawdown in Wednesday's storage report.

As a result, prices for gas flowing into the California at the southern end of the state remained strong. Traders reported closing deals today in the mid-to-high $2.90s per mmBtu, up about 40 cents from November 1 levels.
